ImageDescription.value:
Aluminum (Al) is the # 3 most common element in Earth's crust, after oxygen (O) and silicon (Si). Many common minerals have a significant Al component (for example, the feldspars). Aluminum in its elemental state - "native aluminum" - is an extremely rare mineral.

The # 1 aluminum ore is an unusual sedimentary rock called bauxite (see: www.flickr.com/photos/jsjgeology/albums/72157632279264614/ ). Bauxite contains aluminum minerals, iron oxide minerals, and clay minerals. The Al-rich minerals in a typical bauxite include gibbsite (Al(OH)3), boehmite (AlO·OH), and diaspore (AlO·OH).

Processing bauxite into metallic aluminum is extremely difficult and requires incredible amounts of energy. In the 1800s, this meant that aluminum metal was very rare and valuable - it was worth more than gold. In modern times, ordinary aluminum foil is considered to be almost worthless.

An estimated 1.5 to 3% of all electricity is used to make Al metal from bauxite.
